questions.q: Per this lesson, where do most integration failures actually originate?
options: In the network layer, which is the least reliable part of most integration chains
In a design decision made weeks or months before the failure appears in production, not in a code bug discovered immediately
Exclusively in third-party API outages outside the architect's control
In the choice of programming language used to build the integration
questions.explain: A large share of integration failures trace back to an earlier design decision — a pattern chosen for convenience, an unverified volume assumption, an undefined interface contract — rather than a simple coding bug.

questions.q: Why is silent data loss described as one of the most damaging integration failure categories?
options: Because it always corrupts every record in the dataset, not just some of them
Because it throws a loud, immediate error that overwhelms support teams
Because it produces no error and no alert, so a record simply never arrives and nobody notices until much later
Because it only happens in synchronous integrations, never in asynchronous ones
questions.explain: Silent data loss is dangerous precisely because nothing visibly breaks — a record fails to arrive with no retry and no alert, and the gap is often discovered much later by a customer or an auditor rather than by monitoring.

questions.q: An integration is built against another system's internal field names and internal ID scheme instead of a documented, stable contract. What failure category does this describe?
options: Volume underestimation
Tight coupling to internal implementation details
No agreed-on error contract
Silent data loss
questions.explain: Tight coupling means the integration depends on another system's internal structure rather than a stable published contract, so it breaks the moment that internal structure changes, even if the underlying business meaning hasn't changed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat a successful demo as a red flag rather than reassurance that an integration is production-ready?
options: Demos are always run on outdated software versions
A demo by design uses clean data, low volume, and the happy path, so none of the recurring failure categories have a chance to appear
Demos are typically run by junior staff who are less careful than production operators
Demo environments use a different programming language than production
questions.explain: Volume underestimation, silent data loss, and timing-assumption failures all specifically require conditions a demo doesn't create: real volume, dirty real-world data, and uneven production load. A clean demo can't surface any of them.

questions.q: An integration assumes updates to a record always arrive in the order they were made. What does this lesson say about that assumption?
options: It's always safe, since every integration style preserves message order
Asynchronous systems in particular routinely violate ordering assumptions, and a design that quietly depends on them will eventually break in a hard-to-reproduce way
Ordering only matters for synchronous, request-reply integrations
This assumption is required by every major integration platform and cannot be designed around
questions.explain: Timing and ordering assumptions are a recurring failure category specifically because asynchronous systems routinely deliver messages out of order or with related records missing, and designs that silently assume otherwise fail unpredictably.
